Nonetheless, persistent gender stereotypes affect more than fertility, as they push women away from smaller communities toward the big cities. To encourage women to remain, it is essential to overcome these stereotypes, particularly by raising awareness among men.

Identifying Differences

In Japan, the proportion of children born outside of marriage is relatively low, remaining at around 2.5%. Because the vast majority of children are born to married women, the total fertility rate is roughly equal to the proportion of married women multiplied by the marital fertility rate.

The graph above shows the positive and negative effects of the three factors. It can be seen that the two regions share common trends. Until 2005, the marriage rate was the primary driver of the decline in births, but from 2010, population became the main driver in both regions. The marriage fertility rate, which was a positive contributor through to 2015, became a negative factor in 2020.

To understand why these shifts occurred, I will examine the marriage and marriage fertility rates separately.

Given that university entry among women in areas outside Japan’s main urban centers is projected to keep climbing, it will be essential to design fertility policies that adapt to these changing social realities.
